title: Sun
day_note: Equatorial spin, about 25 Earth days. Not a sunrise.
year_note: The Sun is the center of these orbits.
moons_note: Planets are not moons of the Sun.
cadet: The Sun is the star at the center of this system. It is a huge sphere of hot gas, and its light is what lets us see the planets at all. If the Sun went dark, Earth would not notice for a little over eight minutes. That wait is the light already on the way.
analyst: A G-type main-sequence star. Equatorial diameter about 1,392,000 km, roughly 109 Earth diameters. Mass is about 333,000 Earths, so surface gravity is near 28 g. The equator spins in about 25 Earth days; the poles take longer. Mean distance to Earth is 1 astronomical unit, about 150 million km, and one-way light-time is about 8.3 minutes. Round public figures, not a live ephemeris.

title: Mercury
day_note: Solar day, sunrise to sunrise, about 176 Earth days.
cadet: Mercury is the innermost planet, a small world with almost no air. It finishes a lap around the Sun in about 88 Earth days. Its spin is locked in step with that lap, so a full day-night cycle lasts about 176 Earth days. From the surface the Sun would look large, and it would crawl.
analyst: Equatorial diameter about 4,880 km. Surface gravity about 0.38 g. Sidereal rotation about 59 Earth days. The solar day is about 176 Earth days because of a 3:2 spin-orbit resonance. Orbital period about 88 Earth days. No moons. Mean distance about 0.39 AU. One-way light-time from Earth runs from about 5 minutes to about 12, depending on where both planets sit.

title: Venus
day_note: Solar day, about 117 Earth days. Spin is retrograde.
cadet: Venus is close to Earth in size and wrapped in a permanent cloud deck. Under the clouds the air is very thick, and the ground is hot enough to melt lead. Venus spins backward, slowly. A day there, sunrise to sunrise, lasts longer than many months on Earth.
analyst: Equatorial diameter about 12,104 km. Surface gravity about 0.90 g. Year about 225 Earth days. Retrograde rotation about 243 Earth days; the solar day is about 117 Earth days. No moons. A carbon-dioxide atmosphere drives a strong greenhouse effect. Surface temperature is about 465 degrees C and surface pressure is about 92 times Earth's. Those are round accepted figures, not a weather report.

title: Earth
cadet: Earth is home base for this terminal. Liquid water stays on the surface, the air is breathable for us, and one spin is a day. One trip around the Sun is a year. A single large Moon travels with us. Nothing else in this file is a second Earth.
analyst: Equatorial diameter about 12,756 km. Mean surface gravity is the reference value, 1 g, about 9.8 m/s squared. Mean solar day 24 hours. Sidereal year about 365.25 days. One moon. Mean distance to the Sun is 1 AU, about 149.6 million km. This file is the comparison baseline for the rest of the terminal.

title: Moon
day_note: Sunrise to sunrise, about 29.5 Earth days.
year_note: Sidereal orbit about Earth, not about the Sun.
cadet: The Moon is Earth's companion rock. It keeps the same face toward us because it turns once per trip around Earth. A radio signal at the speed of light needs about 1.3 seconds to cross the average gap. That is the shortest long haul on this terminal.
analyst: Mean diameter about 3,475 km. Surface gravity about 0.17 g. Sidereal orbit about 27.3 Earth days. The cycle of phases is about 29.5 days. Mean distance about 384,000 km, so one-way light-time is about 1.3 seconds. The Moon has no moons of its own. The familiar near side is a lock between spin and orbit, not a painted face.

title: Mars
cadet: Mars is a cold desert world, a little over half Earth's width. Its day is only slightly longer than ours, which is why mission planners talk in sols. Two small moons, Phobos and Deimos, orbit close and fast. A radio note from Earth often takes on the order of minutes, and the exact wait changes as the orbits move. No life has been confirmed there.
analyst: Equatorial diameter about 6,792 km. Surface gravity about 0.38 g. Solar day about 24.6 hours. Year about 687 Earth days. Two moons. Mean orbital distance about 1.52 AU. One-way light-time ranges from about 4 minutes at closest approach to about 21 minutes when Mars is on the far side of the Sun. 12.5 minutes is a mid-range figure, not a fixed clock. Machines on and around Mars are human hardware. This terminal does not track them live.

title: Jupiter
moons_note: More than 100 catalogued around mid-2026. The integer still moves.
source_note: Moon totals are mid-2026 catalogue language and can change.
cadet: Jupiter is the largest planet, a giant of gas with no ground to stand on. It spins fast: a day is under ten hours. Pale bands wrap the globe. They are clouds, not continents. Many moons travel with it. The list of tiny outer moons keeps growing, so this terminal will not pretend the count is finished.
analyst: Equatorial diameter about 142,980 km, about 11 Earth diameters. Equatorial gravity about 2.5 g. Rotation about 9.9 hours. Year about 11.9 Earth years, roughly 4,330 days. Mean distance about 5.20 AU. One-way light-time from Earth is about 35 minutes when Jupiter is nearest in line, and about 52 minutes when it is across the Sun. Catalogues around mid-2026 list more than 100 known moons. That integer changes when small bodies are confirmed. The Great Red Spot is a long-lived storm.

title: Saturn
moons_note: On the order of 300 catalogued around mid-2026. The integer still moves.
source_note: Moon totals are mid-2026 catalogue language and can change.
cadet: Saturn is the ringed giant. The rings are not a solid plate. They are a vast crowd of ice pieces, each on its own orbit, bright because they reflect sunlight. The planet under them is mostly gas, and its day is short. Most of its moons are small. A few, such as Titan, are worlds of their own.
analyst: Equatorial diameter about 120,500 km, rings excluded. The globe is visibly flattened by its spin. Surface gravity about 1.1 g. Rotation about 10.7 hours. Year about 29.5 Earth years. Mean distance about 9.6 AU. The main rings reach well beyond the globe and are only tens of meters thick in many places. Catalogues around mid-2026 list on the order of 300 confirmed moons, most of them kilometre-scale and faint. That total is a survey result with a date, not a constant like the diameter. One-way light-time from Earth is a little over an hour.

title: Uranus
moons_note: 29 in mid-2026 catalogues. Faint moons can still be added.
source_note: Moon totals are mid-2026 catalogue language and can change.
cadet: Uranus is an ice giant that rolls along its orbit. Its spin axis lies almost sideways, so for long seasons one pole faces the Sun. It has thin rings and a family of moons. The core on this page is a shaded greyscale sphere. A measured color in its air is a fact about the gas, not a paint we apply.
analyst: Equatorial diameter about 51,100 km. Surface gravity about 0.89 g. Retrograde rotation about 17.2 hours. Year about 84 Earth years. Axial tilt about 98 degrees. Mean distance about 19.2 AU. Mid-2026 catalogues list 29 known moons; the count can move when faint satellites are confirmed. Methane in the atmosphere absorbs red light, so observers record a pale cyan. One-way light-time from Earth is a few hours.

title: Neptune
moons_note: 16 known. Triton is by far the most massive.
source_note: Moon totals are mid-2026 catalogue language and can change.
cadet: Neptune is the outer ice giant. From there the Sun is still the brightest object in the sky, but daylight is dim by Earth standards. The winds are fast. Triton, the largest moon, orbits backward. Most researchers read that as a captured body, not one that formed calmly in place.
analyst: Equatorial diameter about 49,500 km. Surface gravity about 1.1 g. Rotation about 16.1 hours. Year about 165 Earth years. Mean distance about 30.1 AU. 16 known moons. Triton holds nearly all of the moon system's mass and orbits retrograde. Capture is the standard account, not a demonstration anyone can rerun. One-way light-time from Earth is a little over 4 hours.

title: Pluto
day_note: About 6.4 Earth days, locked with Charon.
moons_note: Five known. Charon is the largest.
cadet: Pluto is a dwarf planet. It is smaller than Earth's Moon, icy, and on a long tilted path that sometimes comes closer to the Sun than Neptune does. It is not one of the eight planets. That is a naming rule astronomers agreed in 2006. Pluto is still a real world, with five known moons.
analyst: Mean diameter about 2,377 km. Surface gravity about 0.06 g. Rotation about 6.4 Earth days, tidally locked with Charon. Orbital period about 248 Earth years. Eccentricity is high, so the distance to the Sun swings from roughly 30 AU to roughly 49 AU. Five known moons. IAU class: dwarf planet. One-way light-time from Earth is several hours and changes along that stretched orbit. This terminal does not campaign for or against the 2006 definition. It states the class in use.

title: Asteroid Belt
day_note: No single day. Ceres, the largest body, spins in about 9 hours.
year_note: Most main-belt rocks orbit in about 3 to 6 Earth years.
cadet: The asteroid belt is a wide zone of rocks between Mars and Jupiter. Stories sometimes show it as a crowded storm of stone you must dodge. In truth the rocks are far apart. A ship could cross the belt and not pass near another rock. The largest body, Ceres, is itself a dwarf planet, about 940 km across.
analyst: Most main-belt asteroids orbit between about 2.1 and 3.3 AU. Their combined mass is only a small fraction of the Moon's. Ceres, diameter about 940 km, holds roughly a third of that mass. The belt is leftover material that never assembled into a planet. Jupiter's gravity is the usual reason given for why growth stopped. A one-way radio time from Earth is on the order of 10 to 20 minutes and depends on which rock you mean.
